question: What is the source of heat for the engine and wing anti-ice systems?

options.text: Engine bleed air
Electrical heating elements
Hot oil from the engine scavenge system
Exhaust gas recirculation

explanation: Both are thermal systems fed from the pneumatic ducts, which is why a bleed failure also costs the airframe its ice protection.

question: Which part of the engine is protected by the engine anti-ice system?

options.text: The fan blades and spinner
The engine inlet cowl lip
The compressor inlet guide vanes
The entire nacelle surface

explanation: Only the cowl lip is heated. The rotating parts shed ice by centrifugal action, so they do not need a heat supply.

question: How is engine anti-ice selected?

options.text: By an individual switch for each engine
By a single switch for both engines
Automatically whenever TAT falls below the icing value
By the wing anti-ice switch when the flaps are up

explanation: Independent switches allow one engine to be protected if the other has a failed valve or a bleed problem.

question: What does a bright blue cowl valve light indicate?

options.text: The valve is closed and the switch is OFF
The cowl has overheated
The valve is open and operating normally
The valve is in transit or disagrees with the switch position

explanation: Bright means the system has not yet reached the commanded state, and the light dims once the valve confirms the selection.

question: What does an amber COWL ANTI-ICE light indicate?

options.text: The valve has failed closed
The switch has been left ON after landing
Low bleed pressure at the valve
An overheat in the cowl anti-ice duct

explanation: Excessive temperature in the cowl can damage the inlet structure, so it is annunciated separately from valve position.

question: What is the effect of selecting engine anti-ice ON at idle thrust?

options.text: Idle N1 decreases
Idle thrust is unchanged
Idle N1 increases
The engine reverts to approach idle only with flaps extended

explanation: Idle is raised so the engine can still supply usable bleed pressure while producing minimum thrust.

question: How does engine anti-ice affect takeoff performance?

options.text: It reduces available thrust because of the bleed extraction
It has no effect on performance
It increases available thrust by warming the inlet
It only affects performance above the transition altitude

explanation: Air taken for ice protection is air not producing thrust, so the takeoff performance calculation has to account for it.

question: Icing conditions are considered to exist when visible moisture is present and TAT is at or below which value?

options.text: Zero degrees C
5 degrees C
10 degrees C
15 degrees C

explanation: The threshold is set well above freezing because of the temperature drop in the accelerating airflow at the inlet. Verify against your operator FCOM.

question: On the ground, icing conditions also exist when the temperature is at or below the threshold and which condition is present?

options.text: Surface water, slush or snow on the ramp or runway
A crosswind exceeding ten knots
The APU supplying both packs
A cabin altitude below field elevation

explanation: Standing water can be thrown into the inlet and freeze there even in clear air. Verify the exact wording against your operator FCOM.

question: Why is engine anti-ice used as an anti-ice rather than a de-ice system?

options.text: Because the system cannot be selected once ice has formed
Because ice shed from an unprotected inlet can be ingested and damage the engine
Because the valves are inhibited above idle thrust
Because the bleed supply is insufficient to melt accumulated ice

explanation: The aim is to prevent an accretion forming at all, since a released sheet of ice entering the core is far worse than the drag of prevention.

question: Which surfaces are protected by the wing anti-ice system?

options.text: All leading edge devices including the Krueger flaps
The three inboard leading edge slats on each wing
The complete wing leading edge
The leading edge and the trailing edge flaps

explanation: Only the inboard slats are heated. The outboard devices are left unprotected because the inboard sections dominate the handling effects of ice.

question: What indicates that a wing anti-ice valve is open and operating normally?

options.text: A dimly illuminated blue valve open light
A bright blue valve open light
An amber valve light
No light at all

explanation: Dim confirms agreement between the switch and the valve, while bright is the transit or disagreement indication.

question: What happens to wing anti-ice when takeoff thrust is set with the switch ON on the ground?

options.text: Nothing, the system continues to operate
The valves open fully to the high flow position
The valves close and the switch moves to OFF
The system transfers to automatic in flight control

explanation: Ground operation is limited so that full bleed is available for takeoff, and the system is then reselected once airborne if required.

question: Can wing anti-ice be used to remove ice that has already accumulated on the ground?

options.text: Yes, it is an approved ground de-icing method
No, ground ice must be removed with de-icing fluid
Yes, but only with both engines at high thrust
Yes, provided the APU is supplying both ducts

explanation: The system has neither the heat nor the coverage to shed a ground accretion, and any melt water can refreeze further aft on unprotected surfaces.

question: Why is wing anti-ice normally selected before ice accumulates rather than after?

options.text: Because the valves cannot open once ice has formed
To avoid the risk of ice being shed into the engines and to keep the protected surfaces clean
Because the bleed demand is lower when the wing is already cold
To prevent the wing body overheat detectors from tripping

explanation: Runback and shed ice from a late selection are the problems the anti-ice philosophy is designed to avoid.

question: What is the main penalty of operating wing anti-ice in the cruise?

options.text: A reduction in maximum cabin differential pressure
Loss of the trailing edge flap protection
Increased fuel burn and reduced performance
An increase in cabin altitude

explanation: The bleed taken from the engines has to be paid for in thrust and fuel, which is why its use is limited to when it is actually needed.

question: Why is a leak in the wing anti-ice ducting a significant hazard?

options.text: It causes an immediate loss of cabin pressure
It prevents the slats from extending
It contaminates the fuel in the wing tanks
It can lead to a wing body overheat and structural damage

explanation: Hot bleed air escaping inside the leading edge is detected by the overheat sensing elements, and the response is to shut off the source.

question: Which windows are electrically heated?

options.text: All flight deck windows
The No. 1 forward and No. 2 side windows
The No. 1 windows only
The No. 2 and No. 3 windows

explanation: Heat is applied where the crew needs a clear view, so the fixed aft window is left unheated.

question: Besides ice and fog protection, what is the additional benefit of heating the forward windows?

options.text: It reduces the glare from direct sunlight
It maintains the electrical bonding of the airframe
It improves the resistance of the windshield to bird strike
It allows the wipers to operate at higher speeds

explanation: Warm laminate is more flexible and absorbs impact better, which is why the forward window heat is selected for takeoff and landing.

question: How many window heat switches are provided?

options.text: Two
Three
Four
Six

explanation: There is a switch for each heated panel, left and right forward and left and right side, so a single failure costs only one window.

question: What does an illuminated green ON light next to a window heat switch mean?

options.text: The window has reached its overheat limit
The window heat controller has failed
The switch is in the test position
Heat is being applied to that window

explanation: The light cycles as the controller applies and removes power, so intermittent illumination is normal.

question: What happens when a window OVERHEAT light illuminates?

options.text: Heating to that window is removed automatically
The window heat transfers to the opposite side
All window heat is lost
The window is isolated from the electrical system permanently

explanation: Uncontrolled heating can delaminate the window or cause arcing, so the controller removes power as soon as the limit is sensed.

question: How does the window heat controller sense the need for heat?

options.text: From the total air temperature probe
From the cabin temperature controller
From ram air temperature at the pack inlet
From temperature sensors in the window laminate

explanation: Sensing the glass itself is what allows the temperature to be held within the narrow band the laminate can tolerate.

question: What is checked by the window heat test positions?

options.text: The continuity of the wiper motors
The response time of the probe heaters
The window de-misting airflow
The overheat sensing and the power circuits

explanation: Testing the protective circuit matters as much as testing the heater, because an undetected overheat is what damages the window.

question: Which of these is protected by the probe heat system?

options.text: The windshield and the side windows
The engine inlet cowl lips
The pitot and static sensing, the TAT probe and the angle of attack sensors
The water and waste drain lines only

explanation: Every air data input depends on an unobstructed sensing port, so all of them are heated as a group.

question: Why is the TAT probe heater not powered while on the ground?

options.text: To reduce the electrical load during engine start
Because the probe is not exposed until the gear retracts
To avoid an erroneously high temperature reading with no airflow over the probe
To prevent damage to the probe from ground handling

explanation: Without airflow the probe would heat itself and report a false TAT, which would corrupt the thrust and icing calculations.

question: What does an amber probe heat light indicate?

options.text: That the heater for that probe is not operating
That the probe has reached its operating temperature
That the probe heat switch is ON
That icing conditions have been detected

explanation: The lights are failure annunciations, so the absence of a light with the system selected on is the normal indication.

question: What is the consequence of an unheated pitot probe in icing conditions?

options.text: Loss of altitude indication only
Unreliable airspeed indication as the probe ices over
An immediate autothrottle disconnect
Loss of the angle of attack indication only

explanation: A blocked pitot corrupts the dynamic pressure sensing, which is the classic origin of an unreliable airspeed event.

question: Why are the water and waste drain masts heated?

options.text: To warm the potable water for galley use
To prevent drain lines and masts freezing and blocking
To prevent the waste tank contents from freezing in the cruise
To maintain the pressurisation seal at the drain penetration

explanation: A frozen mast blocks the drain and can allow an external ice accretion to build up on the fuselage.

question: What selections are available on the windshield wiper control?

options.text: OFF, SLOW and FAST
PARK, AUTO and MANUAL
PARK, INT, LOW and HIGH
OFF, NORM and MAX

explanation: Independent controls for each side allow the pilot flying to run a wiper without distracting the other pilot.

question: Why should the wipers not be operated on a dry windshield?

options.text: The motors will overheat within seconds
The blades will detach at low airspeed
The window heat will be inhibited
They will scratch and damage the glass surface

explanation: A dry wipe drags grit across the outer ply, and the resulting scratches degrade visibility permanently.

question: What restricts the use of the windshield wipers?

options.text: A maximum operating airspeed
A minimum outside air temperature
A maximum cabin differential pressure
A maximum flap setting

explanation: Aerodynamic loads on the blade arm at high speed can damage the mechanism. Verify the limiting speed against your operator FCOM.

question: How is rain removal assisted on the Next Generation windshields?

options.text: By a chemical rain repellent sprayed from a pressurised can
By bleed air blown across the outer surface
By a hydrophobic surface coating
By an electrostatic charge applied to the glass

explanation: The coating causes water to bead and be carried away by the airflow, which is why a separate repellent system is not fitted.

question: What is the primary means of determining that icing conditions exist on a standard airplane?

options.text: An automatic ice detector on the fuselage
Crew assessment of TAT and visible moisture
An ice accretion warning from the air data computer
Illumination of the wing anti-ice valve lights

explanation: The standard airplane has no ice detection system, so the decision rests on the temperature and moisture criteria applied by the crew.

question: Where is ice accumulation on the wing normally checked visually at night?

options.text: Using the logo lights on the fin
Using the landing lights only
Using the taxi light reflection off the nacelle
Using the wing illumination lights on the leading edge

explanation: The wing lights are aimed at the leading edge precisely so that an accretion can be seen from the flight deck in darkness.

question: Why must anti-ice systems be considered before selecting engine bleeds off for performance reasons?

options.text: Because the anti-ice systems are electrically powered from the same bus
Because the packs must be off before anti-ice can be selected
Because the bleed switches are interlocked with the wing anti-ice switch
Because the anti-ice systems depend on bleed air to function

explanation: A bleeds off configuration removes the heat supply, so it cannot be used when ice protection is required.

question: What is the effect on the anti-ice systems of losing an engine in icing conditions?

options.text: The remaining engine can supply protection through the isolation valve
Both wing and cowl protection are lost completely
Only electrical protection remains available
Wing anti-ice reverts to automatic operation

explanation: Joining the two duct sides allows the operating engine to feed both wings and both cowls, which is why the isolation valve logic matters in icing.

question: Why is the use of wing anti-ice on the ground normally avoided in warm conditions?

options.text: Because the valves cannot open below flying speed
Because it interferes with the flap position indication
Because it drains the hydraulic reservoir pressurisation
Because the leading edge structure can overheat without airflow to carry the heat away

explanation: In flight the airflow removes the heat continuously, and without it the duct and skin temperatures rise beyond what the structure tolerates.

question: What is the danger of runback ice forming behind a heated leading edge?

options.text: It blocks the anti-ice ducts from the inside
It accumulates on unprotected surfaces where it cannot be removed
It causes the slats to jam in the extended position
It short circuits the window heat controllers

explanation: Melt water refreezing aft of the heated area builds a ridge on a surface the system cannot reach, which is why partial and late protection is undesirable.

question: Which of the following ice protection functions is electrical rather than pneumatic?

options.text: Window heat
Wing anti-ice
Engine cowl anti-ice
Both wing and cowl anti-ice

explanation: Electrical heating suits the small, precisely controlled areas such as windows and probes, while bleed air suits large structural surfaces.
